stem: Which of these may a COR do?

options.text: Monitor, inspect and report to the contracting officer
options.why: That is the COR's role.

options.text: Change the contract price when the customer agrees
options.why: Only the contracting officer can change price.

options.text: Extend the delivery date by up to 30 days
options.why: Schedule changes are contract changes.

options.text: Direct work that is not in the contract if it is urgent
options.why: That is a change the COR cannot make.

stem: Under the Prompt Payment Act, interest on a late payment is:

options.text: Paid automatically, without the contractor having to ask
options.why: Interest penalties are automatic.

options.text: Paid only if the contractor asks in writing
options.why: No request is required.

options.text: Paid only on invoices over $25,000 that are 30 days late
options.why: There is no such floor in the general rule.

options.text: Never paid by DoW, since DoW is exempt from the Act
options.why: DoW pays Prompt Payment interest like other agencies.

stem: A stop-work order can halt work for up to:

options.text: 90 days, unless both parties agree to longer
options.why: 52.242-15 allows 90 days, after which the order is cancelled or the work is terminated.

options.text: 10 days, unless the contracting officer extends it
options.why: Too short.

options.text: 30 days, after which work resumes automatically
options.why: The clause allows 90.

options.text: One year, or until the funds run out
options.why: Far longer than the clause allows.

stem: A novation agreement is used to:

options.text: Recognize a new company that took over the contractor's business
options.why: The Government is not required to recognize a transfer without a novation.

options.text: Order a change within the contract's scope after a merger
options.why: That is a change order.

options.text: Rate a contractor's performance after a change of ownership
options.why: That is CPARS.

options.text: Resolve a protest about the contractor's ownership
options.why: Protests are handled under Part 33.

stem: What happens with CPARS evaluations?

options.text: Contractors can comment, and later source selections use them
options.why: CPARS records performance for future buyers.

options.text: They are kept secret from the contractor and used only by the agency
options.why: Contractors see and can comment on their evaluations.

options.text: They are used only to decide award fees on the same contract
options.why: Their main use is past performance in source selections.

options.text: They replace the contract file once the contract is closed out
options.why: They are separate records.

stem: In DoW, contractors submit invoices and receiving reports through:

options.text: PIEE Wide Area WorkFlow (WAWF)
options.why: WAWF is DoW's electronic invoicing and receiving system.

options.text: SAM.gov, through the entity registration
options.why: SAM.gov is for registration, notices and award data.

options.text: CPARS, with the performance ratings
options.why: CPARS is for performance assessments.

options.text: Email to the COR, with a copy to finance
options.why: DoW requires electronic invoicing through WAWF.

stem: Which is an exception to the finality of acceptance?

options.text: A latent defect
options.why: Latent defects, fraud and gross mistakes amounting to fraud are the exceptions.

options.text: A patent defect the inspector missed
options.why: Patent defects should have been caught; acceptance stands.

options.text: Any defect found later
options.why: Only the listed exceptions, or contract terms such as a warranty.

options.text: A defect the contractor admits after acceptance
options.why: An admission alone does not create an exception.

stem: A latent defect is:

options.text: A defect that existed at acceptance but a reasonable inspection could not find
options.why: Hidden defects are why acceptance is not always final.

options.text: A defect that is obvious on a normal inspection at delivery
options.why: That is a patent defect.

options.text: Damage caused after acceptance by Government misuse or poor storage of the item
options.why: That is not a contractor defect.

options.text: A late delivery that the contractor did not report in time
options.why: Lateness is not a defect in the item.

stem: If the Government decides to accept nonconforming supplies, it should:

options.text: Get consideration, such as a price reduction
options.why: Accepting less than specified without consideration gives away Government rights.

options.text: Pay full price to keep good relations
options.why: That gives the contractor value it did not deliver.

options.text: Accept without telling the contracting officer
options.why: The contracting officer must handle the decision.

options.text: Always reject them
options.why: Acceptance with consideration can be in the Government's interest.

stem: For commercial products, the Government usually relies on:

options.text: The contractor's existing quality assurance system
options.why: Commercial buys generally rely on the seller's own quality processes.

options.text: Government source inspection at the factory
options.why: Source inspection is for higher-risk items.

options.text: A third-party auditor hired for every commercial buy
options.why: Not required as a rule.

options.text: No quality checks at all, since the item is commercial
options.why: The Government still inspects at acceptance.

stem: For services, where is the Government's surveillance approach written down?

options.text: In the quality assurance surveillance plan (QASP)
options.why: The QASP tells the COR what, how and how often to check.

options.text: In the contractor's proposal and quality control plan
options.why: The proposal describes the contractor's approach.

options.text: In CPARS, with the ratings
options.why: CPARS records results, not the plan.

options.text: In the J&A or the acquisition plan
options.why: A J&A justifies limiting competition.

stem: When should a contract include a warranty?

options.text: When its benefits outweigh its cost, considering the item and trade practice
options.why: Warranties are a cost-benefit decision.

options.text: Always, because warranties come free with every purchase
options.why: Warranties are priced into the contract.

options.text: Never for commercial items, since the market and the seller's policies already cover them
options.why: Commercial items usually come with standard warranties.

options.text: Only for services, where performance is hard to inspect
options.why: Warranties are most common for supplies.

stem: The Government has privity of contract with:

options.text: The prime contractor only
options.why: Subcontractors deal with the prime, not the Government.

options.text: The prime and all its subcontractors
options.why: There is no privity with subcontractors.

options.text: Subcontractors only after consent
options.why: Consent does not create privity.

options.text: Small business subcontractors only
options.why: Size does not create privity.

stem: When the contracting officer consents to a subcontract:

options.text: The prime keeps full responsibility; the Government is not a party to the subcontract
options.why: Consent is a risk-control check, not an approval that shifts responsibility.

options.text: The Government becomes liable to pay the subcontractor if the prime does not
options.why: No privity, no liability.

options.text: Every term of the subcontract is approved by the Government
options.why: Consent is not a blanket approval of terms.

options.text: The prime no longer needs to manage the subcontractor
options.why: The prime still manages its subcontractors.

stem: What does a contractor purchasing system review (CPSR) do?

options.text: Evaluates how a contractor buys from its suppliers; approval reduces consent needs
options.why: CPSRs, done by DCMA in DoW, look at purchasing policies and practices.

options.text: Audits the contractor's indirect rates and its billing system
options.why: That is DCAA audit work.

options.text: Checks the SAM registration and exclusion status of every subcontractor the prime uses
options.why: SAM checks are separate.

options.text: Rates the past performance of the contractor's subcontractors
options.why: That is CPARS.

stem: Who must provide a small business subcontracting plan?

options.text: Large businesses on bigger contracts with subcontracting possibilities
options.why: Plans apply to other-than-small businesses on larger contracts.

options.text: Small businesses that win set-aside contracts above the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: Small businesses are exempt from plans.

options.text: Every contractor on every contract, whatever its size
options.why: Plans apply only above thresholds and to large businesses.

options.text: Only construction contractors working on military bases
options.why: Plans apply to supplies and services too.

stem: A subcontractor says the prime has not paid it in 90 days and asks the Government to pay it directly. What can the Government do?

options.text: It cannot pay the subcontractor directly, but it can press the prime and note it in CPARS
options.why: Without privity, the Government works through the prime.

options.text: Pay the subcontractor directly and deduct the amount from the prime's next invoice
options.why: Direct payment ignores privity and the contract terms.

options.text: Order the prime to replace the subcontractor and pay all of its costs
options.why: That is not the first or proper step.

options.text: Nothing at all, since payment between companies is private
options.why: The Government can still act through the prime.

stem: Who may execute a contract modification?

options.text: Only a contracting officer, within the limits of their authority
options.why: RFO FAR 43.202 limits modifications to contracting officers.

options.text: The COR, for changes under $25,000 that do not affect price
options.why: CORs cannot modify contracts.

options.text: The program manager, when the change is technical only
options.why: Program managers have no contracting authority.

options.text: The contractor, if it absorbs the cost of the change
options.why: The contractor cannot change the contract alone.

stem: Changing the paying office or correcting accounting data is done by:

options.text: An administrative change, which is unilateral
options.why: Administrative changes do not affect the parties' substantive rights.

options.text: A supplemental agreement signed by both sides
options.why: No bilateral agreement is needed for administrative changes.

options.text: A change order under the Changes clause
options.why: Change orders change the work under the Changes clause.

options.text: A novation agreement with the paying office
options.why: Novations recognize a successor contractor.

stem: A change order is:

options.text: A unilateral written order under the Changes clause, within the general scope
options.why: The contractor must comply and may ask for an equitable adjustment.

options.text: A bilateral agreement on a new price for added work
options.why: That is a supplemental agreement.

options.text: A change outside the general scope that the contractor must accept and perform at once
options.why: That would be a cardinal change.

options.text: Any written instruction from the COR to the contractor
options.why: CORs cannot issue change orders.

stem: A modification signed by both the contractor and the contracting officer is a:

options.text: Supplemental agreement
options.why: Bilateral modifications are supplemental agreements.

options.text: Change order
options.why: Change orders are unilateral.

options.text: Administrative change
options.why: Administrative changes are unilateral.

options.text: Stop-work order
options.why: Stop-work orders are unilateral.

stem: A change so large that it falls outside the general scope of the contract is a:

options.text: Cardinal change: new work that needs its own competition or justification
options.why: Out-of-scope work cannot be added by change order.

options.text: Constructive change, which the contractor must perform first
options.why: Constructive changes are informal changes, often within scope.

options.text: Administrative change made by the contracting officer alone
options.why: Administrative changes are minor.

options.text: Minor deviation that the contractor must accept and perform without any extra pay
options.why: Out-of-scope changes are not routine.

stem: A COR insists the contractor add a weekend shift that the contract does not require, and the contractor complies. This may be a:

options.text: Constructive change
options.why: Government conduct that effectively changes the work, without a formal order, can entitle the contractor to an adjustment.

options.text: Administrative change
options.why: This affects the work itself.

options.text: Valid change order
options.why: Only contracting officers issue change orders.

options.text: Novation
options.why: Unrelated.

stem: Which is NOT required before exercising an option?

options.text: The contractor's written agreement to the exercise
options.why: Options are exercised unilaterally by the Government.

options.text: Funds are available
options.why: Required.

options.text: The contractor is not excluded in SAM
options.why: Required.

options.text: Exercising the option is the most advantageous way to meet the need, given current prices
options.why: Required.

stem: Contractor claims above what amount must be certified?

options.why: The Contract Disputes Act requires certification of claims over $100,000.
$50,000 is a board small-claims figure.
That is the SAT.

options.text: $10 million
options.why: Unrelated.

stem: How long does a contractor have to appeal a final decision to the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals?

options.text: 90 days from receiving the final decision
options.why: That is the board appeal deadline under the CDA.

options.text: 12 months from receiving the final decision
options.why: Twelve months is for the Court of Federal Claims.

options.text: 6 years from the date the claim arose
options.why: Six years is for submitting a claim.

options.text: 30 days from the date of the decision
options.why: The board deadline is 90 days.

stem: How long does a contractor have to take a final decision to the U.S. Court of Federal Claims?

options.text: 12 months
options.why: That is the CDA deadline for the court.

options.text: 90 days
options.why: Ninety days is for the board.

options.text: 10 days
options.why: Ten days is a protest timeline.

options.text: 6 years
options.why: Six years is for submitting a claim.

stem: A contractor must submit a claim within how long after it accrues?

options.text: 6 years
options.why: The CDA's six-year limit.

options.text: 1 year
options.why: Too short.

options.text: 90 days
options.why: That is the board appeal window.

options.text: There is no limit
options.why: The CDA sets six years.

stem: While a claim is being resolved, the contractor must:

options.text: Keep performing diligently as the contracting officer directs
options.why: The Disputes clause requires continued performance.

options.text: Stop work until the claim is decided by the board
options.why: Stopping work could lead to default.

options.text: Stop only the disputed portion of the work and keep the rest going
options.why: Performance continues as directed.

options.text: Get GAO's permission to continue the disputed work
options.why: GAO is not involved in contract disputes.

stem: For a certified claim over $100,000, within 60 days of receiving it the contracting officer must:

options.text: Issue a decision or tell the contractor when it will issue one
options.why: That is the CDA rule for larger claims.

options.text: Always issue the final decision, with no extensions
options.why: For larger claims, a decision date can be set instead.

options.text: Forward it to GAO or the board for review
options.why: GAO does not handle claims.

options.text: Do nothing until DCAA finishes a full audit of the claim and the rates
options.why: The 60-day response is still required.

stem: After a termination for convenience, the contractor is generally paid:

options.text: Allowable costs for work done, a reasonable profit on it, and settlement expenses
options.why: That is the basis of a convenience settlement.

options.text: The full contract price, less the cost of work not yet started
options.why: It is paid for work done, not the whole contract.

options.text: Nothing, because the Government ended the contract
options.why: Convenience terminations pay for work performed.

options.text: The profit it expected on all the work, including the terminated work, plus its costs
options.why: Anticipated profit on terminated work is not allowed.

stem: In a termination for convenience settlement, profit is NOT allowed on:

options.text: The terminated portion of the work
options.why: Profit is paid only on work actually performed.

options.text: Work completed before the termination
options.why: Reasonable profit on completed work is allowed (unless the contractor would have lost money).

options.text: Accepted deliveries
options.why: Accepted work is paid at the contract price.

options.text: Any part of the contract
options.why: Profit on work done is allowed.

stem: A cure notice gives the contractor at least how long to fix the problem?

options.text: 10 days
options.why: Cure notices allow at least 10 days.

options.text: 3 days
options.why: Too short.

options.text: 30 days
options.why: The minimum is 10 days.

options.text: 90 days
options.why: Far longer than required.

stem: When is a show cause notice used instead of a cure notice?

options.text: When there is not enough time to allow a cure, such as after the delivery date
options.why: A show cause notice asks the contractor to explain why it should not be terminated.

options.text: Before every termination for convenience, as a courtesy
options.why: Convenience terminations do not need a show cause notice.

options.text: When the contractor is performing well but its costs are rising above the estimate
options.why: It is used for performance failures.

options.text: Only for commercial contracts, which have no cure period
options.why: It is used broadly.

stem: If a termination for default is later found improper, it is:

options.text: Converted to a termination for convenience
options.why: The contractor is then paid as in a convenience termination.

options.text: Cancelled, with the contract reinstated automatically
options.why: The usual result is conversion to convenience.

options.text: Left in place
options.why: An improper default is not left standing.

options.text: Sent to GAO
options.why: GAO does not hear terminations.

stem: After a proper termination for default, the contractor may have to pay:

options.text: The excess costs of reprocuring the work
options.why: Excess reprocurement costs are a key effect of default.

options.text: Nothing beyond losing the contract
options.why: Excess costs can be assessed.

options.text: Double the contract price
options.why: There is no such penalty.

options.text: The Government's legal fees in every case
options.why: That is not a standard effect.

stem: A firm-fixed-price contract (not using simplified procedures) should be closed within how long after evidence of physical completion?

options.text: 6 months
options.why: FAR 4.308, Table 4-2.

options.text: 20 months
options.why: Twenty months is for other contracts.

options.text: 36 months
options.why: Thirty-six months is for contracts needing indirect rate settlement.

options.text: 30 days
options.why: Too short for the standard.

stem: Contracts that require settlement of final indirect cost rates should be closed within:

options.text: 36 months after evidence of physical completion
options.why: Rate settlement takes time, so the standard is longer.

options.text: 6 months after the final invoice is paid
options.why: Six months is for FFP.

options.text: 20 months after the date of physical completion
options.why: Twenty months is for all other contracts.

options.text: When the contractor asks and the audit is done
options.why: The FAR sets the time standard.

stem: Contracts that are neither FFP nor need indirect rate settlement should be closed within:

options.text: 20 months
options.why: That is the standard for all other contracts.

options.text: 6 months
options.why: That is for FFP.

options.text: 36 months
options.why: That is for indirect-rate contracts.

options.text: 5 years
options.why: Too long.

stem: A purchase under simplified acquisition procedures is considered closed when:

options.text: When the CO receives evidence of receipt of the property and final payment
options.why: Simplified buys close on delivery and payment.

options.text: Six months after award, if no claims are pending
options.why: The trigger is receipt and payment.

options.text: After a full closeout audit by DCAA
options.why: Simplified buys do not need audits to close.

options.text: When the COR confirms in writing that the work was satisfactory and the file is complete
options.why: Unrelated.

stem: Which closeout step most directly helps the customer's budget?

options.text: Deobligating excess funds
options.why: Returned funds can be reused while still available.

options.text: Filing the contract completion statement
options.why: Important, but it does not free money.

options.text: Archiving emails
options.why: Records matter, but they do not free money.

options.text: Updating the vendor's SAM record
options.why: The contractor maintains its own SAM record.

stem: When is a contract physically complete?

options.text: When all items are delivered and accepted (or terminated) and no options remain
options.why: Physical completion starts the closeout clock.

options.text: When the last invoice is paid and the funds are deobligated
options.why: Final payment is part of closeout, not the definition of physical completion.

options.text: On the contract's original end date, whether or not delivery and acceptance happened
options.why: Completion depends on delivery and acceptance.

options.text: When the CPARS evaluation is signed by the contracting officer
options.why: CPARS is a closeout step.
